source_text: Certe ne tu quidem adeo desipis, ut dicas peccati traducem post circumcisionem factam esse maiorem; quomodo ergo abundavit post legem, quae nec arguitur in lege nec proditur? At hoc vide, quam sanae intellegentiae concinat, quae peccatum in sola delinquentis voluntate constituit. Usque ad legem dicit Apostolus fuisse peccatum, ut post legem intellegatur fuisse praevaricatio [n363] , promulgata videlicet praecepta transgrediens; atque hoc genere abundavit lege subintroeunte peccatum, quoniam reatui eius de praevaricatione crevit invidia, et opus malae voluntatis, sicut ante legem peccatum erat, ita post legem coepit esse transgressio, quamvis non eo proposito legem Deus tulerit, ut mortales fierent eius sanctione peiores. Neque enim lex peccatum aut causa peccati, sed mandatum sanctum et iustum et bonum [n364] . Verum quia delinquentium pravitas eo se ferro, quo curari debuit, vulneravit obstititque consilio Dei, ut inde periclitaretur, unde debuerat sanari, dicit Apostolus de effectu rerum opinionem divini consilii, quo data lex fuerat, iniuriam pertulisse; et quia non fuit is proventus emendationis humanae, in quem lator legis intenderat, sed in plurimis evenere contraria, eo usque ait profecisse studia peccantium, ut non ob aliud videretur data lex esse, quam ut improbi improbiores fierent et ad peccatum praevaricatio iungeretur.
pass_a_gloss: Certainly not even you are so foolish as to say that the tradux of sin was made greater after circumcision; how therefore did it abound after the law, which is neither accused in the law nor betrayed? But see this, how it sounds together with a sound understanding, which has constituted sin in the will of the one offending alone. Until the law the Apostle says there was sin, so that after the law there is understood to have been transgression, namely transgressing precepts promulgated; and in this kind sin abounded with the law entering under, since from transgression envy grew for its reatus, and a work of an evil will, as before the law it was sin, so after the law it began to be a transgression, although God did not pass the law with that purpose, that mortals would become worse by its sanction. For neither is the law sin or a cause of sin, but a holy and just and good commandment. But because the crookedness of those offending wounded itself with that iron by which it ought to have been cured, and stood against the counsel of God, so that it would be endangered from there from where it ought to have been healed, the Apostle says that from the effect of things the opinion of the divine counsel, by which the law had been given, suffered an injury; and because there was not that outcome of human amendment toward which the passer of the law had intended, but in very many contrary things happened, he says that the pursuits of those sinning advanced so far that the law seemed given for no other reason than that the wicked would become more wicked and transgression would be joined to sin.

lemmas.lexica: LS praevaricatio; Blaise Adam's transgression as example
LS tradux=vine-shoot/layer; Blaise tradux peccati=transmission of sin by descent
LS peccatum=fault, error; Blaise Christian sin
LS voluntas=will, wish; Blaise moral will
LS malum; Blaise malum naturale vs malum voluntatis

pass_b_english: Certainly even you are not so senseless as to say that sin transmitted by descent became greater after circumcision. How, then, did it abound after the law when it is neither accused nor revealed in the law? But see how well this agrees with the sound understanding that places sin solely in the wrongdoer’s will. The apostle says sin existed until the law, so that after the law it should be understood as transgression (Romans 5:13): it crosses commands that have been promulgated. In this way sin abounded when the law came in, because transgression added odium to its guilt. The act of an evil will, which before the law was sin, after the law also began to be transgression. Yet God did not give the law with the purpose of making mortals worse through its enactment. For the law is neither sin nor the cause of sin, but ‘the commandment is holy, just, and good’ (Romans 7:12). Wrongdoers’ perversity, however, wounded itself with the blade that should have healed it, and opposed God’s purpose, so that it found danger where it should have found healing. The apostle says that the outcome of events injured the apparent purpose of God’s decision to give the law. Human amendment did not result as the lawgiver intended; rather, the opposite occurred in very many people. He says sinners’ efforts went so far that the law seemed given for no other reason than to make the wicked more wicked and add transgression to sin.

choices.why: Adam's act of crossing the command; Julian's example of sin, not a transmitted nature.
Julian's polemic target is inherited sin as a natural evil (malum naturale), the vine-layer metaphor, not a later systematic 'original sin' slogan and not soul-traducianism as such.
rejected: original sin (later system as default gloss)
traducianism of the soul (not the load here)
